newsitem.title: USA: Pan Am buys Carnival Air; Carnival owner gets stake.
newsitem.headline: Pan Am buys Carnival Air; Carnival owner gets stake.

text.p: Pan American World Airways, a new company with a venerable name, announced a major expansion Friday, saying it would acquire its larger regional rival, Carnival Air Lines.

Specific terms of the deal, which followed two years of discussion, were not disclosed. But the companies said Carnival Air's principle owner, Micky Arison, would invest $30 million in Pan Am, ending up with about 42 percent of the company's outstanding stock and one of the world's best-known trademarks for his airline.

"Customers are comfortable boarding a Pan Am airplane," Pan Am Chief Executive Martin Shugrue told a news conference. "Not that they're not comfortable boarding a Carnival airplane. But the power of the brand is much stronger with the blue ball on the tail."
"It's a well-recognized name," said Kevin Lydeon, associate director at Fitch Investors Service.

Pan Am also has arranged for a private placement of up to $30 million in a new series of convertible preferred stock, for a total $60 million cash infusion that Shugrue said would go to working capital and for expenses such as redesigning Carnival's jets and possibly toward buying more aircraft.
Pan Am began operations last September with just two airliners. With the addition of Carnival's 27 jets, the combination will have 31 aircraft, and 2,075 employees.
"We don't anticipate any layoffs at all," Shugrue told a news conference. "Neither one of these companies has a 30-year airline bureaucracy to deal with."

Carnival Air, which is not part of Carnival Corp., or its Carnival Cruise Lines, was formed in 1988 and is owned by Air Holding Corp. Arison also is chairman and chief executive of the separate Carnival Corp.

Pan Am, though it has proclaimed itself the successor to the venerable airline, began as a new company when it began flying last September. It has seen its load factor rise to 70 percent in less than six months of operation, Shugrue said.
Shugrue said he expected the acquisition would lead eventually to a larger company than the two as currently combined, but offered few specifics on his growth plans.
"Carnival flies its airplanes fewer hours per day than Pan Am flies its airplanes... We fully intend to fly those aircraft for more hours per day," he said.

Shugrue said Pan Am would like to add flights between New York and Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, and add a Miami-Dominican Republic route. He said it would like to increase its New York-Los Angeles route to more than one per day and add routes to Kennedy Airport in New York and to California from Midway Airport in Chicago.
Carnival now has operations in South Florida, the Northeast, California and the Caribbean. It had about $270 million in revenues last year.

The privately held company does not release financial results, but Arison said it had not been profitable since last May, when Valujet Flight 592 crashed near Miami, killing all 110 people on board and diminishing the confidence of air travelers in newer airlines.
"We had been profitable until the Valujet situation," he said. But he said Carnival had posted consistent profits until then and Shugrue added that Carnival was "recovering nicely."

Last July Pan Am agreed to buy Carnival Air for about $100 million but called off the deal after PanAm examined the carrier's books and sought to rework the terms. Shugrue and Arison would not specify what had changed since.

Pan Am currently has a fleet of four Airbus A300's -- with two more to be delivered in the next two months -- flying between New York and Los Angeles, New York and Miami, New York and San Juan, Puerto Rico, Miami and Chicago, and Miami and San Juan. New York-Santo Domingo service will begin April 6.

The original Pan Am, one of the world's first airlines, went out of business amid a myriad of problems related to competition, its limited route structure, industry deregulation and finally, the bombing of one of its airliners over Lockerbie, Scotland in 1988.

Charles Cobb, a south Florida businessman who is now Pan Am's chairman, acquired the Pan Am name after the company went out of existence. He and Shugrue, a former Pan Am executive and Eastern Airlines trustee, announced plans to relaunch a Pan Am on Jan. 30, 1996.
Pan Am's stock closed down 75 cents at $10.125 Friday on the American Stock Exchange, where it was among the most-actively traded issues.
